correctness.rationale: Generic diagonal weights make monomial systems the complete projective fixed locus. A monomial tuple avoids every projective common zero iff for each coordinate label j some equation is the pure power in that variable: necessity follows by evaluation at the j-th coordinate point, and sufficiency by choosing any nonzero coordinate of an arbitrary projective point. Inclusion--exclusion over missing labels gives the stated alternating sum. Algebraic C* localization gives chi_c of the complement, and additivity gives chi_top of the closed consistency locus. Finite-difference identities yield the m<n and m=n specializations. The packaged checker exhaustively verifies the monomial criterion and formula on a finite grid.

originality.rationale: The archival resultant source treats the square n-equation/n-variable hypersurface and determinant formulas, not arbitrary equation counts or this Euler formula. Vassiliev computes cohomology for non-resultant systems in two variables in affine coefficient spaces, a different quotient and dimensional regime. Later consistency-variety work supplies the natural overdetermined terminology and studies generic consistent zero sets, but the inspected abstract does not state the separately projectivized Euler-complement inclusion--exclusion formula. Targeted semantic and web searches for overdetermined homogeneous systems, consistency varieties, common-zero complements, Euler characteristic, and inclusion--exclusion did not locate an equivalent theorem. The closest own result is the square specialization m=n; it implies only the constant n! slice and not the degree-dependent overdetermined formula.

value.rationale: The result extends the classical square resultant threshold to the full underdetermined/square/overdetermined family of complete homogeneous systems and reveals a sharp phase law. Below threshold the complement is empty; at threshold its Euler characteristic collapses to n! independently of degrees; above threshold it becomes a genuinely degree-sensitive inclusion--exclusion polynomial. For linear systems it specializes to n! times a Stirling number, identifying the fixed-point geometry with surjections. The overdetermined consistency locus is a standard natural object in later algebraic geometry, so this is a family-level invariant rather than an arbitrary slice.
